speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Minister for Social and Family Development for cases of suspected child abuse referred by schools to the Child Protective Service (CPS) (a) what is the procedure for investigation of such cases when the child is not attending school; and (b) in what circumstances will the CPS insist on an in-person assessment of such child or exercise its investigative powers including those under the sections 9, 10 and 12 of the Children and Young Persons Act 1993.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Social and Family Development how does the Child Protective Service make known its services to young children who may be suffering physical or mental abuse by their parents or caregivers and may not have access to telephones, the Internet or any other persons outside their home to report the abuse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Social and Family Development what are the conditions or triggers that will mandate a face-to-face meeting between children and officers from the Child Protective Service, either at home or outside of home, in cases of suspected abuse by parents or caregivers.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF)'s Child Protective Service (CPS) investigates cases involving serious abuse or neglect of children and young persons in accordance with the statutory framework set out under the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA).

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: This is because non-attendance could be due to many other reasons.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: To determine if a case meets the legal threshold under the CYPA, CPS will gather information from the child, family and professionals via phone or video calls.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: CPS must balance multiple conflicting interests when determining what is best for a child.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: CPS is careful in exercising its powers and will only remove a child if it is not possible to keep the child safe within his or her family.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: For less serious cases, CPS will refer the child and family to a Child Protection Specialist Centre, Protection Specialist Centre or a Family Service Centre for follow-up intervention as necessary.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The nature of child abuse is that it is often not easy to detect.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The professionals in CPS and the social service agencies work hard to intervene to prevent further harm, and the fate of every single life matters.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Despite their efforts and that of others at the various touchpoints that children come into contact with, it is not possible to expect that every single case will be detected.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: I hope Members of this House can support the difficult work that they do in your communities and to rally your residents to play their part too.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Residents can support the Break the Silence campaign and attend domestic violence awareness training.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Through these, members of the public are educated on potential signs of child abuse or neglect.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Everyone can benefit from such knowledge, whether as a neighbour, a community volunteer or a grassroots leader.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Those who see such potential signs are encouraged to report their concerns to the National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline (NAVH) at 1800-777-0000.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: We are also educating our children on this difficult topic of abuse in an age-appropriate manner.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Preschoolers are taught how to talk about their feelings and seek help from trusted adults when they feel unsafe or hurt.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: In schools, students learn about personal safety and safeguarding themselves against abuse through their Character and Citizenship Education lessons.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: They also learn help-seeking skills, including the "Signal for Help" hand gesture.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: They are shown the community resources and helplines for them to turn to when their safety is compromised.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: They are also encouraged to look out for their peers and seek help for those who display these signs of distress.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recounted the incident of an 11-year-old girl who passed away at the hands of the stepfather.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It affected me because she was of the same age as my daughter.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate the good work of CPS on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having been volunteering with one of the crisis shelters dealing with domestic violence, I know the workload of CPS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But in this particular instance, the intervention by CPS could have been earlier, had the October interview been in person, at home, or in a Police station.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fatal incident happened just the next month in November.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that investigations are still ongoing, but would MSF review what could have been done better – perhaps borrowing or learning lessons from other jurisdictions by using same-age peer befrienders, or even protection of liability for anonymous reporting by educators, in a suspected abuse case?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps this would prevent and avert such a tragic incident from happening again.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: We also find that youngsters nowadays very much prefer the online textual anonymous kind of platforms that allow them to bring to attention some of the plights and situations they are in.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: So, while I cannot comment on the specifics, I think we can call upon everyone in the House and beyond to do more to raise awareness on this issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there some specific conditions in which the CPS will forcibly enter homes to check on the well-being of children whom they suspect of being abused?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Were there any instances in the past five years where these conditions were met, but the CPS did not do so?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if so, what has MSF done to ensure that such protocols are adhered to in future?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: At the point of a case being referred to the CPS, we will perform an intake assessment.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: And at this point, when we do the assessment, we will make sure that we check for any signs of immediate safety concerns for the child, or whether the parents or caregivers are cooperative at a particular stage of investigations.
